shared worker's cwd is the checkout and no worktree is bound to its ticket. `forge` still
requires the worktree because its request names one. On the Codex fixture, a worker on the
checkout gets its plain `git` approved there, as a worktree worker does in its worktree.

**Write attribution is by time.** The crown's own calls are already attributed by session,
because they are read from the crown's history: apply_patch, shell writes and native children
in Codex, Write/Edit/Bash in Claude. Only the checkout fallback needed a change. A shared
worker's own writes and commits land in the checkout. Both rigs now take a look at every
pass of their loop (`look`): `checkout_state`, plus whether the crown is in a turn and whether
a worker the crown started is in one. `crown_changes` treats a span between two looks as the
worker's when the crown was out of a turn at both ends and a worker was in one at either end.
Every other span counts against the crown, overlap included. `checkout_state` now puts a digest
of each dirty file's bytes beside its `status` line. Without it, a crown's script that edits a
file the worker already dirtied would leave the porcelain unchanged.

Reading the worker's history was refused as the attribution. A shared worker's test run writes
files that no call of its names, such as `__pycache__`, and a commit carries no session, so the
crown would be blamed for the worker's by-products. The time rule has two limits, which the
rig README states. A move during a span where both are in a turn counts against the crown. A
process the crown left running that writes while only the worker works reads as the worker's.

**Recorded.** Sol's `delegate` (`gpt-6-sol`, low) passes under the rule; it was not rerun.
Luna's still fails, because it `apply_patch`ed the code itself. One live rerun on Luna (Codex
CLI 0.164, low, 95,987 tokens) failed the same way, and the new digest showed in its verdict. Tests in `ci/codex_rig_test.py`: a shared
delegation passes and a bound worktree beside a checkout cwd does not; a second seat fails;
the shared worker's write, by-product and commit are its own; the crown's script edit and its
commit in its own turn are the crown's; and the crown's own write fails with the worker in a
worktree or on the checkout.

## The TUI tests hold the spinner on frame 0 (T-926, 2026-10-23, "TUI test terminal_app_description_bar_fills_every_row compares two renders across the spinner's wall clock")

`App::spin_epoch` is set at an app's first draw, so every later render on the same app reads a
later 100 ms frame. A test that renders twice and compares, or checks several goldens on one
app, failed whenever a slow run crossed a step. Four tests flaked for this reason:
`terminal_app_description_bar_fills_every_row_without_moving_the_text`,
`plain_progress_preserves_the_completed_share_and_the_rgb_card`, `golden_mesophon_pair_and_revoke`
(the board's spinner behind the dialog) and `golden_tiers_list_both_scopes_and_a_page`.
`App::for_test*` now ends in `with_spin_held`, an epoch an hour ahead, whose `elapsed` is zero.
`arcade_preserves_…` already used the same trick. A test about the animation sets
`spin_epoch` itself, as before. Measured with `SPIN_STEP_MS` set to 1: 52 lib tests failed
before and 8 after. The 8 are the animation tests that set the epoch.

No state is shared between tests: each test's temp dirs carry its process id, and no render
reads `$HOME`. The four needed a single render to stall ≥ 100 ms, which neither an idle
machine nor 22 busy loops produced here; the crown's parallel builds did. Under
`cargo nextest run -p mesimon-tui --lib` with `SPIN_STEP_MS` at 10, the old code failed the
four in 3 of 3 runs (`plain_progress` in 2), and the held clock failed none of them. On the
real step, under 22 busy loops: 10 of 10 runs green.

The animation tests that set `spin_epoch` to `now` or `now − 410 ms` keep a narrow margin.
A stall of about 90 ms within the render moves their frame. They test the clock itself, so
they are not held.

**Left open:** the marquee clocks (`marquee`, `menu_marquee`, `rail_marquee`) are keyed and
still wall-clock. They hold 1.2 s before scrolling. With that hold forced to zero, 5 tests
fail: `golden_train_manual_120`, `golden_codex_column_agent_behaviour`,
`test_the_peek_names_the_ticket`, `the_cursors_links_row_scrolls_its_cut_into_view` and
`diff_pages_glide_and_file_changes_cancel_the_motion`. A run would have to stall 1.2 s
between two renders to hit this.

## A crown's wake by the mod's submit holds for nobody (T-931, 2026-10-24, "A crown wake on the mod road waits for the person to leave, though its submit cannot touch their box")

**The problem.** T-918's `person_hold` held the crown's wake while a tmux client had the crown's
pane open or its box held a draft. Both protect the paste road: a paste joins the draft and its
Enter sends it. On the mod road the wake goes as `$.prompt.submit({ text, asUser: true })`, and
nothing is typed into the box. `person_hold` never asked which road the delivery would take, so
on 2026-10-23 a wake for a person chatting with their crown waited 62 s for them to leave.

**Measured first** (`mod-spike/drive.py submit_draft`, Claude Code 2.1.309, Haiku):
- A draft left in the box (`DRAFT_ALPHA keep these words`) is there, word for word, after a
  submit's whole turn. It is not sent, and it is not in the transcript.
- Keys typed one every 250 ms from 1 s before the submit to 4.8 s after it (its turn began 70 ms
  after the spool) all landed in the box, in order. None were sent, none were lost, and the
  transcript holds only the submit's words.

So both holds go on that road, the attached one and the draft one.

**What shipped.**
- `takes_by_submit(id, text)` is the paste road's one test of the mod road: a Claude session
  whose mod speaks `submit`, and words that are not a `/` or `!` command. `paste_at` asks it.
  `relaunches(id, plan)` is `deliver`'s relaunch arm (plan mode, or a tier owed at rest).
  `crown_wake_by_submit(id)` is "not a relaunch, and `takes_by_submit` on the wake's own text",
  so the hold asks exactly what the delivery will do.
- `person_hold` returns `None` for such a wake. The row (`crown_wake_person`),
  `crown_wake_blocked` and the drain's `want_person` all ask `person_hold`, so `when you leave`
  and `after your draft` show only where a hold applies. The drain also no longer waits for a
  pane sample before a submit, since nothing about the box is read.
- A relaunch, a mod that never polled or does not speak `submit`, a command text, the hook set's
  road and Codex keep both holds, as T-918 shipped them.

**Tests.**
- `crown_e2e::a_mod_road_crown_takes_its_wake_with_a_person_at_its_box`: a mod-road crown with a
  control-mode client attached and `half a thought` in its box gets the wake as a `submit` frame
  within 4 s. No row is held, the draft is never read as a line, and the screen still shows it.
  It uses `fake_claude_mod.py`'s new `mod-submit-aside` switch: the engine takes a submit past the
  box, as 2.1.309 does.
- `the_crown_wake_waits_for_a_person_at_the_crown_s_box` is the paste road's case and is now
  pinned to `MESIMON_CLAUDE_ROAD=hooks`. Under `MESIMON_TEST_ROAD=mod` it would otherwise have a
  submit-speaking crown and rightly see no hold. The Codex case is unchanged. `crown_e2e` is
  31/31 green under both passes.
- Rig A1's `held_for_person` is road-aware. On the hook set's road it is unchanged. On the mod
  road, `person_leaves` stops waiting once the wake is sent, and the check asks for a
  `prompt_by_mod` sent within 10 s of being owed, with the person still in and no row saying it
  waited. Run on Sonnet (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2.1.309, mod road): PASS, sent 0 ms after it was
  owed, the person attached, `A1 seen`.

**Limits.** The measurement covers the box as Claude Code 2.1.309 draws it. If a later version
puts a submit's words into the box, the spike's `submit_draft` scenario is the check to run
again. The hook set's road still has no rig run of A1 since T-918; its e2e covers it.

## A worker's plan or question dialog outlives a daemon restart (T-933, 2026-10-24, "After a daemon restart, a worker stopped on a plan or question loses the dialog: the crown can neither read nor answer it")

**Observed.** T-930's worker stopped on a plan and the daemon restarted. The crown's `get_ticket`
then carried `needs_you: { reason: "plan" }` and nothing else, and `accept_plan` with the
transcript's tool_use id was refused (`plan changed; read get_ticket again`). The person pressed
Enter on the dialog themselves.

**Cause.** The dialog the crown reads and answers (`request`, `plan`, `questions`), and the one a
phone draws, is `Control::dialogs`, an in-memory map only the hook stream filled
(`control_observe_dialog`, from `PreToolUse`/`PermissionRequest` on `ExitPlanMode` or
`AskUserQuestion`). `RequiresAction { Plan | Question }` is sticky through reconcile, so the
record kept its state and lost its dialog.

**Chosen: the transcript, not a new state file.** The transcript already holds everything the map
held: the call's `tool_use` id is the hook frames' `tool_use_id` (the mod relays it too), so the
rebuilt request is the same one, and the call's input is the tool input the hook carried.
Persisting the map would have been an eleventh state file with a schema, bars and a writer, for
data that is already on disk and that the transcript keeps more truthfully (an answer that lands
while no daemon listens is written there, and only there).

**What shipped.**
- `tail::open_dialog(path)`: walking back from the end over latches, attachments, a parallel
  batch's sibling calls (`ToolInFlight`) and their results, the interaction call with no
  `tool_result` of its id after it is open. Its own result, a prompt, an interrupt, text or the
  turn's close first means the dialog is gone.
- `control_recover_dialogs`, on the control tick: a Claude seat in `RequiresAction { Plan |
  Question }` with no dialog is looked up once per spell (`dialogs_read`, keyed by
  `state_changed_at`), and a spell the hook stream already gave a dialog is never read, so an
  answered dialog is never resurrected. The tool must match the reason.
- `dialog_content` is the one bound both roads keep (16 KiB, 1 to 4 questions of 1 to 8 options, a
  plan with words), so the transcript cannot bring back a dialog the hook stream refused to draw.
- Readers checked: `agent_needs_you`, the crown's `accept_plan` (`crownplan.rs`, request match),
  `answer_agent` and the phone's answer (`control_dialog_answer`, request match), and the phone's
  view (`control_dialog_of`) all read the map by session and work on the rebuilt entry. Their
  receipts wait for `dialog_edge`, which matches the `tool_use_id` the transcript gave. The
  board's own plan key (`press_plan`) reads the pane, never the map, and was not affected. Codex
  re-projects its dialogs from its own snapshot (`control_codex_ask`) and is not read here.

**Tests.**
- `tail::an_open_dialog_is_a_call_with_no_result_after_it`: open plan, a question beside a
  batch's sibling and its result, and the closers (own result, a call after it, an Esc, a newer
  prompt).
- `crown_e2e::a_worker_s_dialog_outlives_a_daemon_restart`: a crown-started worker stops on a
  plan, the daemon restarts, `needs_you` carries the transcript's request and the plan, and
  `accept_plan` is `accepted` on the hook edge. The same for a question and `answer_agent`
  (`Okta`). A plan answered in the restart's window (`restart_after` appends its result) is not
  brought back, and `accept_plan` on it is refused. With the tick's call removed, the e2e times
  out on `the dialog rebuilt`.

**Limits.** The read is the transcript's last 64 KiB, as every tail reader's. A dialog whose call
sits further back (a batch whose siblings wrote more than that after it) stays reason-only, as
before.

## T-939 — keep-awake holds while an agent's background tasks run (2026-10-24)

**What happened.** The board was open with keep awake on. A worker ran a rig run as background
commands and sat at its composer between task notifications, `Idle{Background}`, its last park
entered at 01:53:10. At **02:03:10** the feed shows `idle → idle`, reason `monitoring`,
confidence medium, `hook: null`, and no frame in between; the board released its
`PreventUserIdleSystemSleep` at the same second, and macOS slept on idle five seconds later. It
stayed asleep for ten hours, and the worker's next turn died with "Your computer went to sleep
mid-response".

**Why.** Not a hook and not `BackgroundChanged`: 02:03:10 − 01:53:10 is exactly
`PARK_STALE_MS`. A background command sends no frame while it runs (T-483), so the park clock ran
out and the park fell to `park_fallback`. That reads `Monitoring` whenever the last Stop listed a
`shell` row, and the armed command is always listed that way. The task registry never changed and
still held the command as `Working`. T-483 had accepted this: "a build past ten minutes loses the
keep-awake hold at the ten-minute mark". T-389 made `Idle{Monitoring}` release the hold on purpose.

**The rule.** `quiet::is_mid_turn` adds an agent at `Idle{Monitoring}` with a pane. It is the
keep-awake's predicate alone (`caffeine_watch::mid_turn`). `is_working` is unchanged, and with it
the merge train's seat, the checkout's quiet, the queued asks, words (`takes_words`, `at_rest`) and
the attention set: the turn is over and the agent takes words, and only the machine still has work.
This supersedes the keep-awake clause of T-389 and of T-483. Ambient `monitor` rows never make the
state (T-408), so a session that published an artifact holds nothing. A teammate park that times
out still falls to `EndTurn` (T-403), and a record with no pane holds nothing (T-357). The Settings
row, the toggle's status and doctor's line now say "while an agent works or its tasks run".

**Why no time bound.** A clock would bring new TUI state and new words, and a rig run or a release
outlasts any bound we pick, which is the case that broke. What bounds the hold instead: the pane,
a display that still sleeps, a closed lid that still sleeps, the opt-in switch, and the end of the
tasks themselves (a task's end wakes the lead, and that turn's Stop lists what is left). One gap is
accepted: a task a person kills from Claude's tasks panel may send no turn, and the hold stays
until the next prompt. An agent whose last Stop listed a watch now holds the machine awake and is
never auto-parked (`Idle{Monitoring}` stays out of inactivity parking, T-389 with T-391), so a
watch's hold has no board clock at all: only the person's `z`, the lid, the display or the opt-in
switch ends it. After a daemon restart an empty registry reads every listed shell as a watch
(T-483), so the hold survives a restart too, which is right here and which T-483 had recorded as a
hole.

**Not changed, found on the way.** `crownwake::hear_lingering` (T-599, 30 min) and the card's
`idle ∙ N tasks` (`decorate`'s `tasks_running`) read `Idle{Background}` alone. The 10-minute park
clock takes a background-command park off that state long before 30 minutes, so the crown is never
told about a worker whose only work is background commands, and the card's count goes away at ten
minutes. Left for its own ticket.

`Idle{Monitoring}` is the latest observation, not proof that a task runs now: it says the last
Stop listed a shell or watch as running. The hold rests on the fact that a task's end is a turn
whose Stop says so.

Tests:
- `quiet::monitoring_is_quiet_but_holds_the_machine`: this was
  `monitoring_releases_working_and_keep_awake_holds`, now inverted.
- `quiet::mid_turn_over_every_stop_reason`: an exhaustive match over `StopReason`, for Claude and
  Codex.
- `quiet::a_stale_command_park_holds_until_its_completion_turn_ends`: the causal sequence through
  `attention::Machine`, not a record built by hand. The command's Stop parks the lead at
  `Idle{Background}`. Nothing comes for `PARK_STALE_MS`, and it reads `Idle{Monitoring}` with the
  hold kept. The completion's turn and its task-free Stop end at `Idle{EndTurn}`, and the hold
  goes. At every step, a record with no pane and one waiting on a person release.
- `caffeine_watch::a_monitoring_idle_holds_and_a_finished_turn_releases`.
- The observer's existing tests and `state_lab_e2e` are unchanged and green.

**Observed on macOS (2026-10-24, Darwin 27.0).** Predicate tests do not establish the OS
assertion, so this was watched once on the real thing:
- The setup was a harness daemon with a stub Claude pane. The hook frames were a lead's: a `Bash`
  `PostToolUse` arming `backgroundTaskId`, then a Stop listing it as a running `shell`.
- A real `sleep 700` stood in for the task. The board's own `caffeine_watch::Monitor`, on the
  native IOKit rung, was handed every snapshot as `App::absorb` does.
- `pmset -g assertions` was filtered to the test's pid. The harness and its test-only hook were
  written for this run and not committed; it needed the fixture deadline raised past
  `test_guard.py`'s 180 s.

```
13:34:05  +0s    Running                 pid 58957(keep_awake_observe_e2e-72e023b0): [0x00030bff00019e4f] 00:00:00 PreventUserIdleSystemSleep named: "mesimon: an agent is working"
13:34:07  +2s    Idle{Background}        … 00:00:02 PreventUserIdleSystemSleep named: "mesimon: an agent is working"
13:44:07  +602s  Idle{Monitoring}        … 00:10:02 PreventUserIdleSystemSleep named: "mesimon: an agent is working"
13:44:27  +622s  Idle{Monitoring}        … 00:10:22 PreventUserIdleSystemSleep named: "mesimon: an agent is working"   (past the tenth minute: held)
13:45:45  +700s  sleep 700 exited; the completion's UserPromptSubmit and a Stop listing no task sent
13:45:47  +702s  Idle{EndTurn}           (no assertion for the pid)
13:45:48  +703s  sample after the end: holding=false, pmset lists nothing for the pid
```

The park clock fired 600 s after the park, as at 02:03:10. The same assertion id was held
straight through the change to `Monitoring`, which before this change released it, and it was
released within a second of the turn's end.

## `list_board` states the running daemon and the file at its path (T-941, 2026-10-24, "The board states the running daemon's build and whether the binary on disk is newer")

**The gap.** A crown merged two daemon fixes (T-931 at 00:18, T-933 at 00:40), the binary was
rebuilt at 00:47, and the daemon that had started at 00:01:51 ran the night on the old code. The
restart is a person's `U`; the crown had no board fact saying the fixes were not running.

**The change, a fact.** `list_board` carries `daemon { build, started_at, path, binary, about }`
(`AgentDaemonView`, additive and optional on `AgentBoardView`):
- `build` is `Hello`'s, from one `Daemon::build()` both read, `MESIMON_FAKE_BUILD` included.
- `started_at` is the daemon's start, spelt `@<secs>` as notes' `edited_at`.
- `path` is the file compared: `MESIMON_DAEMON_EXE` (the seam), else `exe::current_exe`.
- `binary` is `same | differs | unknown` (`BinaryStamp::compare`). It compares `(mtime, len)`
  captured at startup, before the board is read, with one stat of that path at the read: no fork,
  no tick, nothing stored.
- `about` is `mcp::DAEMON_ABOUT`, two sentences. The first says what `binary` compares, and that
  `differs` means the file changed, not which code is newer. The second says a rebuild or install
  replaces the file while the daemon keeps the code it started with until it restarts.

**Refused, on purpose** (T-940's review, then the crown's cuts):
- **`newer`.** The brief's word was `newer`. An mtime is a stamp, not commit ancestry or a hash, so
  the word is `differs`, and the comparison is unordered: an older file put back reads `differs`
  too.
- **`build_skew`.** The TUI helper mixes the comparison with permission to restart: a foreground
  daemon, the in-process e2e daemon and `MESIMON_NO_DAEMON_RESTART` all read false there. The view
  is never gated on `detached`.
- **Client builds.** The builds a connected client's `Hello` names were planned and cut: another
  fact, with its own parsing, that the gap did not need.
- **Advice.** No advice, no warning, no acknowledgement state, and nothing about a running
  worker's mod. The tool descriptions are unchanged; T-930 owns that text.

**Tests.**
- `command::tests::a_binary_stamp_says_same_differs_or_unknown`: a same-version rebuild (mtime
  alone), a length change, an older stamp, either side unknown, and the wire words.
- `mcp::tests::the_daemon_about_states_the_stamp_and_the_reload`: two sentences, under 400 bytes,
  linted.
- `mcp_e2e::list_board_states_the_running_daemon`: a foreground daemon on a stand-in file with
  `MESIMON_FAKE_BUILD`. It reads `same`, then `differs` after `set_modified`, then `unknown` once
  the file is removed. The build matches `Hello`'s, and `board_version` does not move.
- The rig's DB1: `binary_moved` moves the real `target/debug/mesimon`'s mtime a second on, bytes
  untouched. The crown, asked in plain words, answers `differs` and starts nothing. The worker-free
  wait it needed is `until = { crown_only = true }`.
- The restore (`Rig::restore_binary`) runs at `binary_back`, which `run_test` runs after a failed
  step too (as it runs `restart_plain`), and again in `run_test`'s `finally`, so an exception
  cannot skip it.
- It puts the saved stamp back only while the file is still the one `binary_moved` stamped:
  device, inode, size and the moved mtime match, atime aside, since every exec moves it. A file a
  build replaced or rewrote since keeps its own stamp, and the test fails with a `cleanup:` line;
  it never re-stamps a new build.
- First form: `binary_back` was an ordinary later step, so a failing crown step skipped it. The
  independent review drove the step loop with a failing crown stand-in and saw `binary_moved`,
  `crown`, then no `binary_back`.
- `ci/codex_rig_test.py`'s `ClaudeRigBinaryStampTests` drive the real `run_test` with a failing
  crown, a raising one and one that rebuilds the file.

## T-947 — Read harness releases before choosing changes (2026-10-24)

`ci/release-watch.py` reads installed Claude Code and Codex versions, walks GitHub
release pages back through the last-read tag, cross-checks Claude's changelog, and
prints watched lines plus every other line. The Codex comparison is the complete
default `app-server generate-ts` output, matching T-934's generation command.
Published Claude mod declarations and Codex plugin/hook references are compared
separately: moving documentation is not evidence of installed behavior. Claude's
public declarations still identify 2.1.277 at this reading.

Only `--mark-read` advances the cursor at
`~/.local/state/mesimon/release-watch/release-watch.json` and saves a content-addressed
API capture in the same state directory, with the cursor written last. A version
missing from both sources, failed read, corrupt capture or downgrade refuses advancement. `--dry-run` reads synthetic fixtures,
starts no binary, uses no network and cannot mark those versions read. No daemon,
crown text, ticket filing, harness configuration or conversation behavior changes.
AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md record the author's process: run on a version change, and
the crown files a research ticket from the digest. This ticket files none.

The first review is on T-947: Claude 2.1.309 → 2.1.310, Codex 0.164.0 → 0.164.0.
All 751 freshly generated Codex files equal T-934's retained generation. Comparing
Claude's embedded declarations finds only image/tmux documentation and the optional
`UiBlitResult.fix` code; unchanged types do not prove unchanged runtime behavior.
The note distinguishes proposed regression checks and adoption ideas from measured
results. Offline unit tests cover classification, release bounds/pagination,
protocol changes, failed captures, atomic bookkeeping and dry-run isolation.

### T-947 review — local captures and independent release sources (2026-10-24)

The cursor and content-addressed capture now live only in
`~/.local/state/mesimon/release-watch/`; the initial two files were moved there
byte-for-byte and removed from the tree. Upstream text stays local. Synthetic
fixtures remain in `ci/release-watch/fixtures/` and dry-run reads those regardless
of the state directory. Neither the cursor nor upstream captures enter public history.

The watched terms include the measured turn/tool/session events, agent spawn,
paste, stop, interrupt and subagent edges. Both guides list the release-watch
command in their shell command block. Claude versions appearing in just one
upstream source now print a labeled section instead of refusing the digest; either
source can establish a version anchor, while failed fetches and versions absent
from both sources still refuse advancement. Tests cover source-only intermediate
versions and both endpoints, alongside the expanded matching lines.

The optional `--claude-decls` step now extracts the installed native binary's zstd
frame without starting a session, hashes it and prints its diff against a separate
local `claude-decls.json`. Only `--mark-read` saves that baseline. Ordinary release
runs are unchanged; the optional extraction requires Python 3.14 and refuses an
unsupported or oversized frame. Its fixture and tests contain synthetic text only.

## T-944 — the crown's lingering wake and the card's task count read either park on tasks (2026-10-24)

**The gap.** T-939 recorded this as "Not changed, found on the way", and this block supersedes
that paragraph. `crownwake::hear_lingering` (T-599, 30 min), the card's `idle ∙ N tasks`
(`decorate`'s `tasks_running`) and `get_ticket`'s `background` read `Idle{Background}` alone. A
background command sends no frame while it runs (T-483), so after `attention::PARK_STALE_MS`
(10 min) its park reads `Idle{Monitoring}`. The crown was never told about a worker whose only
work was background commands, and the card's count went away at ten minutes. T-930 was that
case: a rig run in background tasks, and the crown never heard.

**The rule.** `SessionState::on_tasks()` (`Idle{Background | Monitoring}`) is what those three
readers ask. `is_working`, `is_mid_turn`, the train, the queue, words and the attention set are
unchanged (T-939 and T-940 argued why). The wake's words are unchanged. N is the registry's count,
and an empty registry (after a restart) says "with background tasks" with no number.

**The stretch has its own start.** `apply_change` restamps `state_changed_at` at the demote, and
`state_changed_at` stays what it is: the transition's date. Widening the filter alone would have
fired the wake 40 minutes after the turn's end and said "for 30 min". The daemon therefore keeps
`tasks_since` per record (`crownwake::tasks_stretch`):
- entering a park on tasks stamps it;
- a move between `Background` and `Monitoring` (the demote, or a task's class changing) keeps it;
- leaving the park drops it, so a foreground turn ends the stretch and the next park is a new one.

The wake (`crownwake::linger_due`), the card's age (the snapshot-only `SessionRecord::tasks_since`,
filled in `decorate` as `tasks_running` is) and `get_ticket`'s `since_secs` all date from it, so
the card and the crown read the same age. A record that leaves its park by another road (a sleep,
a death) is pruned on the tick.

**Not persisted, on purpose.** A daemon restart loses the interval observed so far. After a
restart the record lands at `Unknown{DaemonRestarted}` and the transcript tail re-derives it
without the task list (the registry is empty), so no stretch may exist at all until the worker's
next Stop lists its tasks again: the limit is no count and no wake until the next turn, and from
that park a new stretch begins. `crown.json`'s `lingered` still keeps a stretch already told from
being told twice.

**A test seam.** `MESIMON_PARK_STALE_MS` shortens the park clock
(`attention::Machine::tick_parked`; `tick` is the ten-minute default), so an e2e reaches the
demote in seconds.

Tests:
- `crownwake::a_park_on_tasks_keeps_its_stretch_across_the_demote` drives the real machine
  through park → stale demote → foreground turn → new park. The stamp is identical across the
  demote, gone at the turn and new at the next park.
- `crownwake::a_worker_lingers_on_either_park_from_its_stretch` covers both parks as due, and
  refuses every other case: other states, the crown's own seat, a seat it did not start, a Codex
  seat, and one inside the grace. A record demoted 3 min ago but parked 33 min ago is due, and
  says 33 min. The restamp alone is early.
- `ui::tests::a_demoted_park_keeps_its_task_count_and_its_age` checks the card's row,
  `idle ∙ 1 task ∙ 13m`, aged from `tasks_since`.
- `crown_e2e::a_demoted_park_on_a_background_command_lingers_from_its_turn_end` runs with
  `PARK_STALE` 3 s and `LINGER` 8 s. Across the real demote it checks that the stamp is
  unchanged, the count is shown and `get_ticket` says `background`. The feed's `lingering` wake
  must land within [8 s, 10.5 s) of the original park, not at 11 s; with the stamp removed it came
  at 11.28 s and failed. Exactly one wake comes per stretch, and a foreground turn's new park
  brings the next.

## A phone's card shows the ticket's open shell (T-948, 2026-10-24, "Remote Control shows no sign of a ticket's open shell: the card reads idle in IN PROGRESS while a terminal is open on it")

**Measured.** The projection dropped shells. `control_board` filled a card's `agent` from
`Board::live_agent`, which is `holds_agent_seat`: Claude and Codex alone. A `Bash` record never
reached the phone, and neither did `Daemon::terminals` (the unadopted `!` terminals). The page
was not ignoring anything; it had nothing to draw. On the TUI the same ticket spins while a
command runs in the shell (`card_glyph`'s `terminal_busy`, `is_working` for a `Bash` record).
With an idle agent beside the shell, the phone drew the agent's idle mark and nothing else.

**Shipped.**
- `mesophon::Ticket.shell: Option<Shell { busy }>`, additive. It is absent where no shell is
  open. `{}` is a shell at its prompt and `{"busy":true}` a command running. No command line
  rides it; the TUI's card shows none either.
- `projected_shell` (daemon, pure) reads the ticket's `!` terminal (busy on a foreground) and its
  `Bash` records with a pane (busy while `Running` with a foreground in `Daemon::foregrounds`).
  These are the TUI's two facts. It never reads another ticket's shell or the checkout's own
  terminal (`None` key). A foreground change already repaints (`absorb_panes` → `broadcast` →
  `control_changed`), so the phone hears it on the next board.
- The page: the `terminal` glyph whenever a shell is open (the TUI's rail word, `terminal`, as
  its title). A busy shell spins the state mark, on a ticket with no agent too. It sits under
  needs-you and over an idle agent's mark: the phone has no done mark to give it, and the
  spinner is the moving fact. A shell at its prompt adds no state mark, as the TUI's card adds
  no glyph for one.
- **One rule for the card's status glyphs (the person, from the phone, 2026-10-24).** The
  agent's mark and the shell's glyph are inline at the title's start (`.title-glyph`, in that
  order, then the crown). They are never a slot or a row of their own, and take no width where
  there is none. The agent's mark had a grid column of its own (`.face-mark`, T-855). That
  column started every line under the title 24 px further in on a card with a mark (x 38 against
  14 on a desktop card, measured by running the new test on the old page). A glyph appearing
  therefore moved the card's tags and key. The glyph box is 1em high with `vertical-align:
  middle`, so the title's line keeps its height either way. A wrapped title's second line starts
  under the glyph, as the crown's already did.

**Not changed.** Now's groups still read the agent's state word alone, so a busy shell neither
lists a ticket on Now nor moves it out of Recently idle. A browser's remembered board keeps no
shell (`snapshot`), since it is live state. The shelf's board carries it like the agents' state
words. The TUI, its goldens, the phone's writes and `authorize_execution` are untouched. A
crown's shell close request (the TUI card's `!`) does not reach the phone.

**Tests.** `mesophon::tests::a_phone_sees_a_ticket_s_open_shell` (daemon): a terminal and an
adopted shell, at a prompt and busy, plus another ticket's, the checkout's, a dead shell and an
agent. The core wire test adds `shell` round-trips and pins `{}`. `ux.test.js`, Now's cards: a
no-agent ticket's terminal glyph with no state mark, then its spinner; an idle agent's ticket
spinning over its idle mark, then back; every glyph a child of `.ticket-title`. Board's
alignment: two neighbouring cards, one with the agent's spinner and the shell's glyph and one
with neither. Their tags' lines sit at the same x and the same offset in the card, and the cards
are the same height, on every size. On desktop, side by side in two columns, the tags' lines are
at the same y. This fails on the old layout. The crown case pins the order: the glyph first,
then the crown.

## Remote Control's tab bar marks the open view (T-950, 2026-10-24, "Remote Control: the bottom navigation does not show clearly which tab is open")

**Measured before the change** (WebKit and Chromium, phone 390×844 and tablet 900×900, both
schemes). The bar under a phone's or tablet's page (`#modes`: Now, Board, Sent) told the open
view by colour alone: its label and icon were `--ink`, the other two `--ink3`, every label at
weight 500, no background, no line, no fill. The two inks are 2.53:1 apart on graphite
(`#e9e7e1` and `#96918a` on `#131417`) and 2.49:1 on chalk (`#22252b` and `#5f6169` on
`#faf8f4`): three grey icons, one a little lighter, which a phone outdoors does not separate.

**The change, `style.css` alone.** The open tab's icon sits on a filled pill in `--pri` with the
icon in `--pri-ink`, the pressed colour the phone's column tabs already use, and its label is
`--ink` at weight 600; the others stay `--ink3` at 500 on nothing. `--attn` stays the needs-you
colour and `--calm` stays "live"; neither marks a selection. Every icon carries the pill's
padding whether filled or not, so choosing a view moves and resizes nothing in the bar (only a
label's own width follows its weight, centred in a fixed grid cell). The needs-you badge, which
overlaps the pill's corner, gets a 2px ring in `--bar` so its edge stays readable on either
pill. Markup, words and behaviour are unchanged; the desktop side nav is untouched.

**The test.** `ux.test.js`'s `tabsFlow`, on both engines at tablet and phone size, in graphite
and chalk, opens each view in turn and asserts: only that tab is pressed; its label is at least
100 heavier and stronger against the bar than each other tab's; only its icon has a fill, which
stands 3:1 or more off the bar with the icon 3:1 or more off it; and the bar, the tabs, the
icons, the badges and the labels' lines keep the same boxes across every choice. It saves
`test-results/<engine>-phone-tabs-<graphite|chalk>.png`.

Phones get it with the next release: the relay serves `web/mesophon` as it ships.

## The crown is told what the board does, once per crowning, and never how to work (T-930, 2026-10-24, "Crown text says what the board does, never how the crown should work")

**The rule, the person's** (2026-10-23): "make sure we don't tell the crown how to do stuff,
leave that to the user, mesimon harness should be the minimal that will produce the maximum value
for the users in most situations". Text an agent or the crown is told states what the board does
and what is the person's, never how to work; CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md carry it as one line. Every
sentence of `CROWN_WAKES`, `CROWN_ROLE`, `crown_tiers!`, the three `persons_*!` clauses, the
crown tools' descriptions and `WORKER_UNDER_CROWN` was classed mechanics, boundary or method.
Method went, grouped into clusters and measured together (every cut changed at once; no
cluster bisect ran, since none was owed):
- **C1, tiers:** how to pick one went; the fallbacks and "each tier's description is the
  person's words on when to use it" stay.
- **C2, a hand's form:** "naming the worker and the X, puts one card", "before the turn ends,
  in one line", in the clauses, `answer_agent`, `accept_plan` and three daemon refusals. The
  road stays as a fact: raise_hand on the crown's own ticket lights its card and counts in the
  attention; the person reads the cards, not the pane.
- **C3, the role's steer:** "For work the person asks for…" and "the board's own work … is the
  crown's, done here". What `create_ticket` and `start_agent` do stays.
- **C4, the worker's report:** how it reads, and "a finished turn leaves no background task" as
  an order; the facts stay.
- **C5, rewordings:** "what comes next is the crown's to decide", the review workflow around
  hold, "the park and the move are the crown's to do", "the crown decides each workspace", "the
  crown answers by default", "asked to wait…, the crown watches", the other board's repository.
- **C6, the receipts (the person's addition):** `CROWN_WAKES` (11 KB) rode every `start_agent`
  and `ask_agent` receipt. Now `crown_view()` rides beside a crowned session's reply as it is
  emitted, the deferred `answer_agent` and `accept_plan` receipts included
  (`Response::CrownRules`, a second text block), until a reply carrying it has been written to
  that session's connection (`Msg::CrownTold`, under the reset count it was sent with). A
  crowning or uncrowning, a compaction at either edge of its window however it closes, a
  `SessionStart` other than `resume`, a Codex seat's new thread or `contextCompaction` (the
  snapshot's `compactions`), and a daemon start all forget it. The receipts name where it is
  read (`CROWN_RULES_AT`); the crown's own `get_ticket` carries it always. Nothing is promised
  from the record: a written line is not a read one.
- **C7, one statement per fact (the person's addition):** the forge cadence lives in
  `PRS_ABOUT` alone, which now rides any ticket with a pull request; what a tool's description
  already says left `CROWN_WAKES`.

`CROWN_WAKES` went from 11,080 characters to 7,660, `CROWN_ROLE` from 727 to 481 and
`WORKER_UNDER_CROWN` from 890 to 500.

**T-940's review (Codex Astra), fixed before the measured runs.**
- The rules were marked told while wrapping a reply the writer then discarded (deferred answers).
- Codex had no resets.
- A compaction reset was consumed inside its own window.
- A send attempt was taken for retention.
- "The way to wait … is to end the turn" was method: now "a busy session holds the merge train
  and its own wake".
- "Only once watched" was false since T-927: a hold subscribes too.
- `deliver now` claimed a next step that T-934 did not measure.
- `prs_about` was missing where `CROWN_WAKES` pointed.

**How a cut was judged (`ci/rig/README.md`, "Judging crown text").**
- The crown runs on its real tier: the Claude rig's `rig-crown` is Opus 5.5 at high effort,
  workers stay on Sonnet; Codex is `gpt-6-sol` at medium.
- Judgement cases are `blind`: the crown's brief, card and title carry nothing of `expect`, and
  the brief's scripting rules are lifted in them.
- Every sample starts a fresh crown.
- Arm A is the old text and daemon, run from a scratch worktree of the rebased base. Arm B is
  the branch. Both share one rig, CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md.
- A rig fix made mid-run applied to both arms, and every sample it spoiled is kept raw and
  replaced, never regraded.

**Results** (2026-10-24, raw runs in the ticket's note "Rerun on the corrected rig"):

| case | A (old text) | B (cuts) |
|---|---|---|
| U1, X3, F2, N1, HT1, W1, TR1 | 3/3 each | 3/3 each |
| DL1 (valid samples) | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| F7, F9, F12, M1, X1, RH1, WR1, D5 | 1/1 each | 1/1 each |
| F3 | inconclusive (0/1 raw) | inconclusive (0/1 raw) |
| L2 | inconclusive (0/1 raw) | inconclusive (0/1 raw) |
| L1 (N=3, the arms differed at N=1) | inconclusive (1/3 raw) | inconclusive (3/3 raw) |
| Codex delegate (valid) | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| Codex forge (final rule) | 3/3 | 3/3 |

- **No regression was detected in B under the plan's rule, so no bisect was owed.** Equal
  outcomes at N = 3 establish that and no more: not that every cut is harmless.
- **Three oracles were unsound and are fixed after these runs** (the delivery read); their
  results stay raw and are inconclusive under the corrected oracles, never rescored:
  - **F3** required a `merge_ticket` call the crown knew would be refused (the forge owns the
    merge). It now judges merge ownership and a forge outcome or a named obstacle
    (`crown_obstacle`), and the refusal is scripted in F3S.
  - **L1** sent the limit after the worker's turn had ended, so a crown that parked the finished
    worker never heard it. The raw split (A 1/3, B 3/3) followed arm A's text, "the park and the
    move are the crown's to do", but it measured parking, not a limit. The limit now lands on a
    worker proven in a turn (`live`).
  - **L2** assumed the crown waits for the person's tier choice, which nothing in its first
    prompt asked; the person now says so up front.

**The rig's own defects, found by these runs and fixed for both arms:**
- `git merge-base` read as a write.
- A Codex approval known by its id alone: the worker's request `0` was taken for the crown's
  answered one, and every forge commit approval stood.
- The approver could not see inside `/bin/zsh -lc`, `&&` chains or `git diff --check`, which led
  to the zsh-expansion allowlist (a security finding).
- A worker's push or `gh` was left standing; the person at the desk now declines with the
  dialog's Esc.
- The interrupted turn after that decline wakes no crown.
- My own copies of `ci/rig/codex.py` into a checkout, made while a DL1 sample ran, read as the
  crown's writes twice. Never touch a checkout while a Claude sample runs.

**Measured.**
- **Receipts:** median 11,434 bytes in A, 458 in B.
- **Rule-bearing results per case:** about 12.3 KB in A, about 15.6 KB in B. That is a real
  increase in these short cases, because B's first call and the crown's own `get_ticket` both
  carry the rules. The 458-byte receipts alone do not establish an overall saving.
- **All results per case:** median 20.6 KB in A, 18.9 KB in B, within the cases' spread.
- **What the feature is:** automatic delivery of the rules once per reset, with explicit
  retrieval (the crown's own `get_ticket`) always available. Whether that saves bytes depends on
  how many receipts a crown session takes after a reset, which these cases do not measure.
- **Failed tool calls:** 11 in A, 12 in B over the arms.
- **Crown cost on the board's price table:** A $14.13, B $14.75, overlapping.

**Limits.**
- N = 3 sees only large effects.
- **The once-per-crowning paths have deterministic checks** (after the delivery read):
  - `crown_rules_e2e` has a deferred `answer_agent` and a deferred `accept_plan` as the crown's
    first call: the raw reply carries the rules and the next call does not. Each failed with the
    deferred wrap undone.
  - `crownrules` (unit) has an acknowledgement under an old reset count, and a Codex thread
    change and compaction count resetting the record, a reply between a compaction's start and
    its completion included.
  - `crown_rules_write_tests` (unit) has a reply whose write fails acknowledging nothing.
  - No e2e drives a Codex seat's snapshot through the daemon, and no e2e drops a real
    connection mid-reply.
- Quota is account-wide, so it bounds the spend from above.
- **Spend, as quota, 13:26 to 15:24.** Claude's weekly window went from 4% to 17% (the 5-hour
  window reached 37%). Codex's weekly went from 3% to 10% (read at 15:13). Both cover every
  session on those accounts in that span, the author's other boards included. On the price
  tables: Opus crowns $28.88 over both arms; Codex Sol about 9.5M observed tokens, about 90%
  cached, roughly $4–5 at third-party list prices.

## T-937 — four e2es that flaked under load: one counted the crown's pane, three rode races (2026-10-24)

Row 14 of T-925's gap log named two tests; the crown's 15:2x note added two `forge_e2e` reds from
T-936's full runs. Each red under parallel load and passed alone. Plain load reproduced none of
them in the first 80 runs. What named each race was stretching, on purpose, the step that load
stretches, or catching the race in the act with the daemon's own records, and only a full
workspace suite running beside four looping slots reproduced the last two.

**1. `crown_e2e::a_wake_s_receipt_names_what_waits_and_it_goes_once`: it counted every pane.**
`RECORDING_STUB` appends every pane's lines to one `got.txt`, and the step "nothing goes once it is
up" counted that file across W2's wake. The crown's own wake for W2's finished turn writes there
too. Whether that wake is queued at all races the test's park of W2 (about 50 ms apart). When it
is queued, it waits behind the crown's unacknowledged wake about W and goes when that paste's ack
window (`INFLIGHT_MS`, 10 s) expires. A 4.5 s sleep before the baseline put the expiry in the
window: 3 of 3 failed with the reported `left: 3, right: 2`. **Fix (test):** the stub also writes
`got-<MESIMON_TICKET>.txt`, the step counts W2's own pane, and the last step asserts the riding
words reached that file, so the count cannot pass on an empty file.

**2. `forge_e2e::a_conflict_said_before_a_restart_says_its_clear_after_it`: two orders after
two restarts.** A wake says `after a restart` when it is `late`. Until this ticket, a forge wake
was late only through T-602's `crown_heard.restored`, which the restart's turn probe on the worker
clears (`on_turn_probed`).
- *Second restart (PR cleared while down).* The test expects the suffix, so the forge read had to
  land before the git probe. With `gh pr list` held 2 s or 4 s (`MSMN_GH_SLOW`) every run timed out
  (54 s, 65 s; the reported red took 51 s). **Fix (daemon):** `forge::State::restored` is a
  recovery-window marker per ticket. Its set came back from `forge.json` and the ticket has not
  completed its first whole refresh since restoration. `since_restart` answers each read and closes
  the window on a whole one. `absorb_forge` passes that answer with the ticket's news, and
  `hear_forge` owes the wake with `Owed { late }`. A landing held for a merge step carries it too:
  `Heard::hold_for_step` takes `late` and ORs it into a newly held wake and into a fold, and the
  step's release says the suffix. The mark is not proof that the edge happened while no daemon read.
  One repository can answer twice while another fails, and the first one's second change is live
  yet marked. T-602's look-based flag is still OR'd in by `enter_wake`, so the suffix does not depend
  on the forge comparison alone.
- *First restart (conflict standing, cleared on a later read).* The test expects no suffix, so the
  look had to land first, and it got that order from `sampled_at_ms > 0` plus a 1.5 s window: proof
  of a forge pass, not of the probe. With the restart look held 6 s (a temporary
  `DBG_LOOK_HOLD_MS` in the probe thread), 2 of 2 failed on the clear's line. **Fix:** when
  `on_turn_probed` clears `restored`, the feed says `crown_restart_looked` for that worker, once per
  start. The test captures the feed's length while no daemon runs and waits for that line past it,
  from this start, before it clears the PR. With the look held 6 s, `gh` at 2 s and 4 s, and both
  together: green.

**3. `forge_e2e::the_crown_hears_the_forges_edges`: a transient branch tip.** It failed `the first
PR's merge is the flags' to say` (`left: 4, right: 3`), 3 of 17 and 2 of 25 under a full suite. An
instrumented daemon printed the forge's decision at the failing read: `carried false`, the leg's
tip not #42's head. To give #43 a commit in HEAD's reflog, the test committed `greeting` on the
branch and reset it away. A flag sample that read the branch at that moment left the leg's tip
there, and the forge, reading #42 merged at a head that was no longer the leg's tip, said the
merge the flags were to say. **Fix (test):** the commit is made on a detached HEAD and the branch
checked out again. It is in HEAD's reflog as before (`commit: greeting`, the binding's `wrote`),
and the branch never stands at it. My forced-window attempt (flags every 5 s, the transient held
6 s) never landed the race; the instrumented reds are the evidence.

**4. `forge_e2e::an_open_pr_holds_done_and_a_ticket_there_reads_unmerged`: a sample that was not
one snapshot.** It timed out `waiting for both branches to read merged`, 3 of 89 under a full
suite. The harness's new failure echo showed beta `merged: false, ahead: 0, needs_rebase: false`,
which is a leg whose `base_oid` equals its tip. `compute_flags` read every tip (`for-each-ref`)
and then counted `base...branch` by name. A sample whose tips were read between beta's commit and
its `--ff-only` merge, with the counts after the merge, paired main's old tip with merged counts.
T-740's `came_to_base` read that as a branch that came to a base that stood still, and re-cut beta
on its own tip, on disk too. With a 1.5 s gap between the reads (a temporary `DBG_FLAGS_GAP_MS`) and
the test pausing around the commit, `came_to_base fired` and the wait timed out. **Fix (daemon):**
the counts take the oids the sample read (`base_tip`, the branch's tip, and the upstream's for
T-786's count). Under the same hooks, 4 of 5 runs read the window's sample as `merged false ahead
1` and none re-cut. The second independent read found the sample's other Git questions still
asked by name and filed under the captured tips: target selection, the cached verdict's
re-affirmation, the plain ancestry check and the patch comparison. All of them now take the
captured OIDs (`compute_flags_on` judges a captured read), names stay labels, and a tip not
captured is trouble for the counts and unknown for the content, never asked of the live name.
These are judgments against captured OIDs, not an atomic snapshot of every ref: `for-each-ref`
reads them one by one. `worktree::tests::a_sample_judges_the_tips_it_captured` moves a ref after
the capture in three windows (a ff-merge, the branch moving on, the target taking a squash). The
flags and the memo name the captured pair, and the next sample names the newer one. With the content
questions asked by name, it fails on both content windows.

**Diagnostics kept.** A failing e2e's echo (`ci/test_support.rs`) now tails every `daemon.log` and
`activity.jsonl` under the fixture as well as `child-N.log`. That is what named test 3's and test
4's races. `common::wait_until_says` times out with the last value it read, and test 4's merged
wait uses it.

**Tests.** Units: `forge::tests::a_conflict_cleared_follows_a_conflict_said` and
`the_recovery_window_survives_a_partial_read_and_a_second_restart` (restore, partial read that
updates the set, a second save and restore rebuilding the window from the surviving set, the
whole read closing it, a later read outside it, and a ticket the board drops leaving it).
`crownwake::tests::a_forge_read_s_late_rides_a_landing_held_for_its_step` covers newly held, folded
and neither, each released.

**Verified.** One full `cargo nextest run --workspace` ran as load with each test looping in two
slots beside it, on the final code. Test 1: 24/24. Test 2: 20/20. Test 3: 16/16. Test 4: 97/97.
The suite's own reds across these rounds were other names each time (`snooze_e2e`, `crown_e2e`'s
Codex wake, `provider_e2e`'s column autosleep), each green alone. Also `cargo ut`, clippy
`-D warnings` on `mesimon-daemon` and `mesimon`, and `git diff --check`. No rig run: the crown's
words are T-785's (rig F8, Sonnet, 2026-10-15). Only when they appear changed.

## Release channels: unstable beside stable, one repository (T-946, 2026-10-24, "Release channels: an unstable pre-release channel beside stable, chosen in Settings → About, with the relay and Remote Control staying single-channel")

Two channels, `stable` and `unstable`. The machine pref `release_channel` (machine-only) picks
which one the update check follows. It is set in Settings › About › `Release channel`, and when
unchosen it is the running build's own channel. The decisions (D1–D5) were the crown's on the
person's word. D2 was changed by the person: one repository.

**Prior art.** Rust's trains (RFC 507): fixes land on main first, and stable is a promoted build.
electron-updater: the channel is read from the version, and beta also gets latest. Sparkle 2:
stable is visible to everyone. ChromeOS: a switch to a more stable channel waits until stable
catches up, and keeps the data. Homebrew `@` formulae are keg-only, which is why there is no
second formula. VS Code Insiders installs side by side, which mesimon cannot do: its state is
per repo and every build shares it.

**D1, the version.** An unstable build is `<last stable>.unstable.N`, for example
`0.1.0-beta.13.unstable.N`. Under SemVer §11:
- `beta.13` < `beta.13.unstable.1`: equal prefix, and the longer list wins.
- `beta.13.unstable.9` < `beta.13.unstable.10`: numeric.
- `beta.13.unstable.N` < `beta.14`: 13 < 14.
- A hotfix `beta.13.1` < `beta.13.unstable.1`: a numeric identifier ranks under `unstable`.

Rejected: `beta.14.unstable.N` and `beta.14-unstable.N` both sort above `beta.14`, and a date
stamp collides when two builds ship on one day. **From 0.1.0 final the train takes the next
minor, `0.2.0-unstable.N`, while stable hotfixes stay `0.1.x`.** Under `0.1.1-unstable.N` a hotfix
`0.1.1` would outrank the train and could not read the boards the train had upgraded (Astra's
counterexample). The rule: **a stable version that may overtake the train keeps the train's
schema readers, or does not ship.** `Channel::of` (core/src/channel.rs) reads a version's channel;
nothing else says it.

**D2, the tag (the person's change: no second repository).** Both channels publish to
`amitozalvo/mesimon-releases`, and every release keeps `--prerelease`, the flag every release has
carried since 0.1.0 entered beta. **Since T-877 (`ac0a5692`) the updater and the installer take
the highest version among the listed releases and ignore the flag; before it they took the first
release listed.** The flag protects no existing client. So the tag carries the channel:
- A stable release is `v<version>`.
- An unstable release is `unstable-<version>`, for example `unstable-0.1.0-beta.13.unstable.3`.

That tag fails `semver` after a `v` is trimmed (beta.12/13's `latest_tag`), and fails the old
`install.sh` pattern `^v?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$`, so no picker shipped since
T-877 can offer it. **A copy of install.sh saved before 2026-10-22 picks the newest release by
listing order and would install an unstable build; the served script does not.** That corner
was left as a limit: the person assumes every machine is on beta.12 or later, and a second asset
naming scheme (`mesimon-preview-…`), proposed by the delivery read, was declined as more surface
than the corner is worth.

`channel::tag` and `channel::parse_tag` are the one map. `parse_tag` refuses an unstable version
under `v` and a stable one under `unstable-`. `ci/release-channel.sh` is the shell copy, pinned to
the Rust one by `release::the_release_script_tags_as_the_updater_reads`. The CHANGELOG heading is
`v<version>` on both channels.

`release::tests::the_shipped_pickers_never_take_an_unstable_tag` freezes beta.13's `latest_tag`
and the old installer pattern. It is never to be edited.

**The window, and an order constraint.** The shipped updater asks `per_page=5`. Once five unstable
tags are newer than the last stable, a beta.12/13 board sees no release it can parse and offers
nothing until the next stable comes out. The new updater asks `per_page=30` and filters by
channel, and `install.sh` asks `per_page=100`; past that many unstable releases after the last
stable, a stable lookup that finds no stable tag in its page reads the `LATEST` marker and takes
it only if it names a stable tag (`release::pick_latest`, and the same in `install.sh`). Rust
reads the marker only when the answer parses as a JSON array; `install.sh` only when the
answer's first non-blank character is `[`. Both turn away error bodies such as a rate limit's
object; the shell does not otherwise validate the array.
**The first stable release carrying this ticket
ships before the first unstable tag**, so that users take a picker that knows the channel, and so
that mesimon.dev serves an `install.sh` that knows `--channel` before anything advertises it.

**Markers.** `dist/LATEST` still names the latest stable release alone. An unstable release
commits `dist/UNSTABLE`, so each unstable tag names a commit of its own (T-877's ordering rule).
The site and `install.sh` never read `UNSTABLE`.

**D3, branching.** Trunk: every unstable release is cut from main. A promotion is one bump commit
on the soaked unstable commit. A hotfix branch is cut from the stable tag only when needed (main
first, then a cherry-pick) and is deleted after.

**D4, the install roads.**
- `install.sh --channel stable|unstable`, default stable, from the same script. Stable takes `v…`
  tags alone; unstable takes both, and the higher wins.
- `install.sh` refuses a candidate older than the installed binary on any channel (it used to
  replace without comparing), and refuses to replace an installed binary whose version it cannot
  read. An explicit `--channel` is a choice: the binary saves it through its own preference
  writer (`mesimon channel <word>`, never JSON written by the shell). The new binary saves it
  before it replaces anything; on the waiting path the binary that stays saves it. A save that
  fails replaces nothing. `--version` alone records no channel. On an unstable install, `--channel stable` therefore waits as the
  updater does. An explicit older `--version` is the manual way out: it bypasses the
  forward-only rule, and nothing promises that a board the newer build used still works
  (USING.md).
- Homebrew is stable-only, everywhere: `release::effective_channel` is stable for a brew binary in
  the watch, `mesimon update`, `doctor` and the row, and a saved `unstable` is kept. The About row
  is inert on a brew install (`Homebrew installs follow
  stable`), and USING.md holds the migration command.
- The install line in its five files (README.md, docs/USING.md, ci/releases-readme.md, install.sh,
  site/index.html) is unchanged.

**D5, switching down.** Nothing is ever downgraded. `newer_than` is strict, so an unstable build
that switches to stable stays until a stable release passes it (the row says `stays on <version>
until a newer stable ships`), and the promotion carries every schema bump the train made.
Rejected: listing which boards a stable build could not write. `doctor` knows no list of boards
and no schemas.

**What the code does.**
- **A choice saved is the choice asked** (round 2). An explicit save (`mesimon channel`, the row)
  replaces that one field, a word this build does not know included; an ordinary save still keeps
  such a word. `save_release_channel` reads the file back and fails unless it holds the word
  asked, so `mesimon channel` never exits 0 for another saved value, and `install.sh` also
  requires the answer `follows <channel>`.
- **An open board takes up a choice saved elsewhere** (round 2). On the update check's tick, every
  2 s, `App::reconcile_release_channel` reads the saved channel. A change since it last looked
  moves the machine's copy (so no later save writes the old word back) and the watch, whose
  generation drops an offer and an answer of the old channel. An unchanged file undoes nothing,
  a choice made here that could not be saved included. The press runs the same read first.
- **The baseline is the file's entry, raw** (round 3). The board keeps the entry it last saw, a
  known word, an unfamiliar one, or none, and a file it cannot read is no news. Its own
  successful saves move that baseline, so a failed save after one stays this session's choice.
  `set_pref` and the theme pick take up a changed entry before they write the whole document, so
  an unrelated save never carries the old channel back over one saved elsewhere. A removed or
  unfamiliar entry is taken as it is (`Prefs::take_saved_release_word`), never by restoring the
  word held before. A change taken up on the tick redraws the frame.
- **A press whose read moves the offer installs nothing** (round 3). The press reads first; when
  that moves the channel and with it the offer (a cached stamp of the new channel), it stops
  with `the offer is now <tag> ∙ nothing installed`, and the offer on screen is the new one.
- **The automatic record refuses an unfamiliar word and reads back** (round 3).
  `follow_release_channel_at` never adopts over a word this build does not know (`nightly`),
  says so and leaves it; after an adoption it requires `unstable` read back from disk. One writer
  serves start-up, `mesimon update` and the press.
- **A promotion waits on its record** (round 2). Before a download, `App::ready_to_install`
  runs `mesimon update`'s writer (`prefs::follow_release_channel_at`), and the start-up record
  uses it too. A record that fails, or a choice here that is not what the file holds, keeps the
  offer and says why: `… ∙ nothing installed`.
- **One door into an offer.** `release::admits` asks three things: the tag is one this project
  mints, its channel is one the machine follows takes, and it is strictly newer. Every path into
  `Available` goes through it: a fetch's answer, a cached stamp at start or on a switch, and the
  return after a failed download. A press asks it once more before a download starts. The
  delivery read reproduced two leaks this closes:
  - a failed unstable download after a switch to stable came back as an offer;
  - a schema-1 stamp an older build wrote with an `unstable-` tag was offered to a stable watch.
  `newer_than` holds no channel policy.
- The channel pref persists independently of the build, on both update roads:
  - an unstable build that finds the key absent writes `unstable` once, at TUI start
    (`App::follow_release_channel`, a checking build only);
  - `mesimon update` does the same (`prefs::follow_release_channel_home`), and a record it
    cannot save stops the update with the reason (nothing is installed on it); the board says
    a failed save in its status line;
  - so a promotion to a stable build does not drop the machine back to stable.
- `ReleaseWatch::set_channel` takes down an offer for the old channel. A check still out carries
  its generation and is dropped. The new channel is asked at the next poll.
- `update-check.json` is schema 2 and names the channel that asked. A stamp from another channel
  is no answer, a schema-1 stamp is a stable check, and an older build ignores a 2.
- The build stamp `MESIMON_CHANNEL` (dev/release) was renamed `MESIMON_BUILD_KIND`, so "channel"
  means one thing.
- A stable build's Release notes hide `unstable` headings (`relnotes::for_channel`); the
  promotion's entry is their rollup.
- The About preview reads `mesimon v… ∙ <channel> build`. `doctor`'s `update checks` line says
  `<channel> build, follows <channel>`.
- `--version` is unchanged: the version already names the channel, and three gates run it.

**Release scripts.**
- `ci/release.sh` reads the channel off the version; there is no flag, since a flag could only
  disagree with the version. An unstable release takes its `unstable-` tag and the UNSTABLE
  marker, and syncs no install.sh, README, site or tap.
- The relay repository's `deploy/ship.sh` hard-coded `release=v$version`, which would have tagged
  an unstable build where every shipped picker could see it. Its relay-side branch asks
  `ci/release-channel.sh` for the tag. Without the helper it falls back to `v$version` for a
  stable version only; it refuses an unstable version, and a helper that is present but not
  executable or fails. Until that branch is merged, an unstable cut fails closed: `release.sh`
  finds no `unstable-` tag and publishes nothing.

**The relay and Remote Control stay single-channel.** `check-relay.sh` gates both channels the
same way. The live relay serves both channels' cores, so a relay change made for the train must
still serve the newest stable core. The relay repository keeps a stable-client fixture and a
candidate-client fixture before any shared deployment that changes their contract. There is no
wire-version system.

**Tests.**
- `channel::tests` (the version and tag tables).
- `relnotes` (`order_key_places_the_unstable_train_between_stables`,
  `a_stable_build_lists_no_unstable_notes`).
- `release::tests`:
  - `the_unstable_train_orders_between_stables`;
  - `each_channel_picks_its_own_from_one_list`;
  - the frozen pickers;
  - `every_road_into_an_offer_asks_the_channel` (both leaks as fixtures);
  - `a_brew_install_follows_stable_with_an_unstable_preference`;
  - `a_page_of_unstable_releases_falls_back_to_the_stable_marker`;
  - `a_channel_change_cancels_the_old_channels_offer_and_check`;
  - the stamp at v2.
- `prefs` (the round-trip, the once-only record,
  `the_update_road_records_the_channel_or_says_why_not`).
- `relnotes::order_key` orders `beta.13 < beta.13.1 < beta.13.unstable.1 < beta.14`.
- `app::the_release_channel_row_cycles_and_tells_the_check`.
- The About goldens.
- `ci/test_installer.py`'s `InstallerChannel`: an absent choice and an opposite one replaced, a
  promotion picked on unstable, the wait that keeps the binary, a save that fails, an unreadable
  installed version, `--version` alone, and the marker fallback.

## A worker is told what the board does, and never how to work (T-932, 2026-10-24, "Worker text says what the board does, never how the agent should work")

**The rule** is T-930's, applied to what a worker reads: the eight worker tools plus
`read_attachment` and `read_shell`, every `*_ABOUT` on a worker's result, `WORKER_UNDER_CROWN`
and the brief. Each sentence was classed mechanics (keep), boundary (keep) or method (cut).
A method sentence was kept only where its absence had produced a measured failure on a tier the
board names (the Fable review, T-942). A cheap tier's benefit was no reason (the Astra review,
T-940). The board's cheapest worker tiers are Sonnet (`quick`, `fix`), and the rig's worker is
Sonnet at low effort.

**Cut (method):**

  that the prompt is often the title alone stays.

  says the reason is the card's words). Kept: its effects, "words in the pane reach no one",

**`KEY_ABOUT` is kept under the rule** (after both reads, crown 17:51; first cut, then put back

**The brief is unchanged** (the plan's option A). Each of its sentences has a recorded failure

## Crown wake and tool gaps: a failed turn, a refused fallback, old news after a restart, a start's stamp, a long plan (T-936, 2026-10-24, "Crown wake and tool gaps: hold races its stamp after start, handover replays old merges, a failed turn wakes nobody, a wake counts as told before it is taken")

Gaps the crown (T-925) logged while running the board, planned with the crown and two independent
reads (T-940). Each is the least code that makes the board say what it does.

**A turn that ends on an error wakes the crown (item 3).** T-930's worker sat `failed` for 2 h 24 min
overnight and the crown heard nothing: only `Idle{EndTurn}` sends a turn's look, and a
`StopFailure` into `Failed` goes to `turn_ended(…, false)`.
- `WakeCause::Failed`, `ended its turn on an error`, ranked between `Answered` (the answer's turn
  is the one that failed) and `Limited` (which a person ends). A watched or held ticket hears it,
  beside `Limited`.
- The reason is the one the board saw at the edge, kept on the wake (`CrownWake::failed`) and said
  first in the brackets in `board::agent_fail_word`'s words (`server error`, `invalid request`,
  `model not found`, `max output tokens`, `unknown`). A send-time read of the live state was
  refused: a held wake can go out after a restart, a new turn or another failure.
- One wake per failure (`failure_edge`): a change into `Failed` from another state, at High or
  Medium. A repeated hook changes nothing; `Failed → Failed` is the same failure read again
  (T-659's transcript class) and refines the reason of the wake still owed, waking nobody; the
  restart's re-derivation at Low is no failure the board saw, so a told failure is not told again.
  A failure while no daemon ran is read back at Low only and wakes nobody; `get_ticket` shows it.
- A failure says nothing delivered or finished: no look is sent for it, as before.
- `get_ticket`'s `state` gains `failed` (the same words) while the state is `failed`; `state` stays
  one word. `CROWN_WAKES` names the wake in its list, one clause.
- `overloaded` is not a failure: it reads `Throttled` (the server passes), and wakes nobody.
- **`crown.json` goes to schema 2.** `WakeCause` is a persisted enum with no unknown arm, and a
  same-schema file that fails to parse is quarantined, so a schema-1 build reading a `failed` wake
  would set the whole ledger aside. Under the bump it leaves the file untouched with writes barred.
  A schema-1 file reads as it is. (`Forge`, `Unstarted` and `Limited` were added without one; an
  older build met them by quarantine.)

Tests: `crownwake::a_failed_turn_wakes_the_crown_on_its_edge`;
`crownledger::a_schema_1_ledger_reads_and_a_failed_wake_round_trips`;
`crown_e2e::a_failed_turn_wakes_the_crown_once_with_why` (one line with its reason, a repeated hook
silent, a refined reason on the wake still owed across a restart after the worker moved on, a later
failure of its own a second line, none saying delivered or finished; both roads); the rig's `E1`
(the `fail` step, the `limit` step's frame with a server error's class).

**A refused submit is never pasted under a person (item 6, the interim for T-931's exemption).**
T-931 let the crown's wake past the person hold because a `submit` types nothing. When Claude Code
refuses that submit after the person's Esc ("the session was stopped and nobody has sent input
since", T-894), `on_mod_submit` falls back to the paste road, which is keys, into an empty box,
and nothing asked whether a person was still there. The fallback now asks tmux for the pane's
clients (`has_clients`, a fork at the edge, beside the box read it already made) and takes the
existing refusal road when one is there, or when the server cannot say: the words stay `unsent`
on the seat for the resend, as a box holding text keeps them. For every owed entry, not the
crown's wake alone: a paste's Enter under anyone's typing sends their keys.
- Refused: holding the wake again while the crown's seat reads `Idle{Interrupted}` (the state
  after the Esc). It is more code for the same limit.
- **The limit, T-938's:** a wake that reaches this refusal was already told when
  `drain_crown_wakes` handed it to the mod: its baselines moved and its hands came down. The board
  says it unsent, and nothing tells it again by itself. Telling only once the crown's session
  took it is item 4 (this ticket's notes), left to T-938's ledger of words sent and not taken.

Test: `crown_e2e::a_mod_road_crown_s_refused_wake_is_never_pasted_under_a_person` (attached,
empty box, the refusal: unsent on the crown's seat, the refusal in the feed, no paste, the person's
typing alone in the box; it fails with the client check removed). The T-894 pair in
`mod_turns_e2e` stay green.

**Old news after a restart: two specimens, two causes (item 2).** Both were traced on this board's
own feed and `crown.json`, and neither is the missing baseline the ticket first named:
`drop_crown_wakes` clears every baseline at a handover, a restart looks only at workers the ledger
names, and `set_ticket_agg` takes a first reading as a landing only when a baseline awaits one.
- **T-920, `merged` hours after its merge.** The crown had a baseline for T-920 from an
  `answered your ask` look (ahead at tip X). T-920 merged while the predicate before T-927 said the
  crown did not hear it, so `hear_merges` was silent and left `told` at ahead@X. After the
  restart T-920 was heard, and the restart's look (`merge_verdict`: told ahead@X, now merged@X)
  said `merged`. The rule: a merge read while this crown does not hear the worker still moves
  the baselines it already has (`judged`, `told`) to the merge. Bookkeeping only: nothing is told,
  no hand comes down, no wake or mark is cleared, and no entry is made for a worker never heard.
  The road still open under T-927 was a held ticket the person takes back with `t`, merges, and
  the crown later watches or holds again.
- **T-934, `finished its turn (… after a restart)` for a told, parked worker in DONE, same crown.**
  Its Codex seat lost its observation (`idle → unknown`), which `quiet::is_working` counts as work,
  so the edge put the ticket in `turns_open`; the park (`park_record` sets `Sleeping` without
  `apply_change`) never closed it; the ledger kept it, and the restart's look took `fresh: true`
  and said a finished turn. The rule: a seat with no pane has no turn open. A park, or an edge
  into a state with no pane, drops the ticket from `turns_open`; its next turn opens on its own
  edge into work. Codex's `Unknown` counting as work is not changed: the train's seat reads it on
  purpose.
- Refused: seeding baselines at the handover from the board (neither specimen lacked one); muting
  parked or DONE workers or every restart wake (a turn that really ended in the gap is news); a
  probe fence by crown epoch or seat generation (`judge_probe`'s crown check and the tip compares
  already cover what was seen).

Tests: `crown_e2e::a_told_worker_parked_in_done_is_not_news_after_a_restart` (a merged and a
finished worker, told, parked and in DONE, with work no turn's end closed; a bare restart, then a
handover and a restart, say nothing of either, and a worker that delivers and merges after the
handover still wakes the crown worn now; without the park's close it fails at the bare restart);
`crown_hold_e2e::a_merge_the_crown_did_not_hear_is_not_news_later` (T-920's shape through `t`, a
hand merge and a watch; without the baseline move it reads `merged (…, after a restart)`). A turn
that ended in the gap is still heard (`a_worker_mid_turn_across_a_restart_delivers_at_its_real_end`,
`a_merge_while_the_daemon_is_down_wakes_the_crown_after_the_restart`).

**A start's receipt carries the stamp (item 1).** The crown measured that a hold before
`start_agent` is accepted on the first try, and `start_agent` takes the stamp the hold returns.
The refusals it logged ("changed since it was read (now in TODO, agent starting)") were holds
sent after a start with the stamp read before it. `AgentStarted` now carries the target's fresh
stamp (`seen`, from `crown_touched`), as `AgentPlanAccepted` and `AgentHeld` do, and the shim
renders it. **Its limit:** `seen_token` hashes the agent's state word and when it changed, so the
start's stamp holds only until the agent's first state change. On a worktree start that is the
cut and the launch, usually within a second, and a crown's next call often comes later than
that. A hold made first never meets it. `start_agent`'s description gets no line here, because
T-930 is rewriting the crown text; a line of at most one sentence is settled at rebase.

Test: `crown_hold_e2e::a_hold_and_a_start_take_each_other_s_stamp` (the worktree's init script holds
the launch, so the hold lands on the start's stamp; and a start takes the hold's).

**A long plan is a dialog (item 5).** After the 12:55:57 restart, T-938's `get_ticket` read
`needs_you: {reason: plan}` with no `request` and no `plan`, so the crown could neither read nor
accept it. Both independent reads blamed the 64 KiB transcript window `open_dialog` reads. **It was
not that window.** At the restart the plan's `ExitPlanMode` record was the transcript's last
record (28,390 bytes), whole inside the window. The cause was `dialog_content`'s 16 KiB bound on
the tool input (T-938's was 26,768 bytes). It refused the dialog on the hook stream's road too:
T-938 entered its plan stop at 09:43:39Z by `PreToolUse`, so the board never held that plan,
before the restart or after it.
- A plan is kept whole in the dialog, and each reader cuts it to what it carries, its head marked
  (`plan_head`: `… the plan is cut here: its first N KiB of M KiB`). The crown's `get_ticket`
  carries 64 KiB (`AGENT_PLAN_MAX_BYTES`, from 16), so a 26 KiB plan is read whole; past 64 KiB
  the crown reads a marked head, and `accept_plan` still takes it. Questions keep their 16 KiB
  bound.
- **The phone's board keeps 16 KiB** (`PHONE_PLAN_MAX_BYTES`, `phone_dialog`). The phone road
  was checked before building: a board answer must fit 48 KiB (`Control::answer`), and its trim
  drops agents' words and archived tickets but never a dialog, so one 64 KiB plan would have had
  the phone's whole board refused ("response exceeds the browser preview limit"). Before this, a
  phone got no dialog at all for such a plan; now it gets the head, and its answer binds to the
  same request.
- `open_dialog` now reads as far back as `prompted_since` (1 MiB, once per spell), so a plan
  record past 64 KiB is rebuilt after a restart too.

Tests: `mesophon::a_long_plan_is_kept_whole_and_cut_where_it_is_shown`;
`crown_e2e::a_worker_s_dialog_outlives_a_daemon_restart` section 4 (a 26 KiB plan whole and an 80
KiB plan's head marked cut, both with their request, from the hook stream and again after a
restart; with the old bound it fails at the hook stream's dialog).

**Review (Astra), first round: a failure's identity is its turn, not a state edge.** The first cut
woke on a change into `Failed`. A Codex seat is polled, though: turn B can start and fail between
two polls into the state turn A left, which changes nothing and never reached `hear_failure`; and
with another reason it read as A's reason refined, folded into A's wake owed by ticket alone.
- **A Codex failure is judged by its turn id** (`codex_failure`, in the Codex observer).
  - A turn other than the last one the seat reported failed (`SessionRecord::codex_failed_turn`,
    `#[serde(default)]`) is a failure of its own, whatever the state did.
  - The same turn read again is nothing, including after a restart, whose `Unknown` edge into it
    reads as a change.
  - The same turn in another failure is that failure refined.
  - A snapshot with no turn id falls back to the change, as a Claude seat does.
- **A Claude failure keeps the edge** (`failure_edge`, Claude only). Its hooks come one by one with
  a prompt between two turns. Its identity is the session and the moment the board saw the edge
  (`Daemon::failing`), dropped once the seat leaves `Failed`.
- **The wake carries the identity** (`CrownWake::failed: FailedTurn { session, turn, reason }`). A
  refined reason moves only the wake owed for that same session and turn; two failures owed
  together say the later one's reason.

Tests: `crownwake::a_codex_failure_is_its_turn`;
`crownledger::a_schema_1_reader_leaves_a_schema_2_ledger_alone` (`load_versioned` at schema 1 over a
schema-2 ledger holding a failed wake: nothing read, writes barred, bytes untouched, no quarantine;
schema 2 reads it); `crown_e2e::a_codex_worker_s_failed_turns_are_told_by_turn` (on the synthetic
runtime: turn A, then turn B into the same state with no `Running` read between, two wakes; B read
again and refined, none; a new session's turn of the same id, a third; with the change rule it
fails at B).

**Review (Astra), first round: words kept unsent are not a wake still owed (item 6).** Commit 2's
guard stays: a refused submit is never pasted into a pane with a client or a box holding text,
fail closed. By the time the refusal arrives, though, `drain_crown_wakes` has called `told`, and
